---
title: "Interest, democracy and trust"
description: "How interested young people in the UK are in politics, how satisfied they are with democracy, and how much they trust its institutions."
date: 2026-11-24
categories: [Democracy, Trust, Age, Gender]
image: thumbnail.png
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "site.R"))

share <- \(x) percent(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 1)

# interest: fairly or very interested
respondents <- respondents |>
  mutate(interested = as.integer(polint) >= 3)

interest <- respondents |>
  summarise(share = share(interested), .by = dataset) |>
  deframe()

interest_gw2 <- respondents |>
  filter(dataset == "Gallup W2") |>
  summarise(share = share(interested), .by = age) |>
  deframe()
interest_gw2_group <- respondents |>
  filter(dataset == "Gallup W2") |>
  summarise(share = share(interested), .by = age_group) |>
  deframe()

# Survation W1 respondents who took part again, and the others
interest_sw1_panel <- respondents |>
  filter(dataset == "Survation W1") |>
  summarise(share = share(interested), .by = panel) |>
  mutate(panel = if_else(panel, "panel", "others")) |>
  deframe()
n_sw1_panel <- sum(respondents$dataset == "Survation W1" & respondents$panel)

interest_gender <- respondents |>
  filter(gender %in% c("Female", "Male")) |>
  summarise(share = mean(interested), .by = c(dataset, gender)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = gender, values_from = share) |>
  mutate(gap = Male - Female)
interest_gap <- number(range(interest_gender$gap) * 100, accuracy = 1)

# satisfaction with democracy
swd <- respondents |>
  summarise(
    satisfied = share(swdkep1 >= 5),
    dissatisfied = share(swdkep1 <= 3),
    neutral = share(swdkep1 == 4),
    .by = dataset
  )
swd_stat <- \(ds, column) swd[[column]][swd$dataset == ds]

swd_gender <- respondents |>
  filter(gender %in% c("Female", "Male")) |>
  summarise(satisfied = share(swdkep1 >= 5), .by = c(dataset, gender))
swd_g <- \(ds, g) swd_gender$satisfied[swd_gender$dataset == ds & swd_gender$gender == g]

swd_gw2_age <- respondents |>
  filter(dataset == "Gallup W2") |>
  summarise(satisfied = share(swdkep1 >= 5), .by = age_group) |>
  deframe()

swd_by_interest <- respondents |>
  filter(polint %in% c("Not at all interested", "Very interested")) |>
  summarise(satisfied = share(swdkep1 >= 5), .by = polint) |>
  deframe()

# trust
institutions <- c(
  trust1 = "Courts",
  trust2 = "Police",
  trust3 = "UK government",
  trust4 = "Political parties",
  trust5 = "Media"
)

trust <- respondents |>
  filter(dataset != "Survation W2") |>
  select(dataset, age, age_group, gender, starts_with("trust")) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("trust"), names_to = "institution", values_to = "trust") |>
  filter(!is.na(trust)) |>
  mutate(institution = institutions[institution])

trust_means <- trust |>
  summarise(mean = mean(trust), .by = c(dataset, institution))
tm <- \(ds, inst) number(trust_means$mean[trust_means$dataset == ds & trust_means$institution == inst], accuracy = 0.1)

trust_gallup_age <- trust |>
  filter(dataset %in% c("Gallup W1", "Gallup W2"), age_group %in% c("18-21", "22-26")) |>
  filter(institution == "UK government") |>
  summarise(mean = number(mean(trust), accuracy = 0.1), .by = c(dataset, age_group)) |>
  mutate(group = str_c(dataset, " ", age_group)) |>
  select(group, mean) |>
  deframe()

trust_gender_gov <- trust |>
  filter(gender %in% c("Female", "Male"), institution == "UK government") |>
  summarise(mean = number(mean(trust), accuracy = 0.1), .by = c(dataset, gender)) |>
  mutate(group = str_c(dataset, " ", gender)) |>
  select(group, mean) |>
  deframe()

# ways of governing: rated fairly or very good (5 to 7)
good <- respondents |>
  summarise(
    both = share(aut1_UK >= 5 & dem1_UK >= 5),
    across(c(aut1_UK, dem1_UK), \(x) share(x >= 5)),
    .by = dataset
  )
gd <- \(ds, column) good[[column]][good$dataset == ds]
```

```{r}
#| label: thumbnail
#| include: false
# Card image for the listings: the interest lines of the first figure,
# without text
thumbnail <- respondents |>
  summarise(share = mean(interested), n = n(), .by = c(dataset, age)) |>
  filter(n >= 20) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = share, colour = dataset)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dataset_colours, guide = "none") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = brand[["tint"]], colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(24, 30, 24, 30)
  )

ggsave("thumbnail.png", thumbnail, width = 6, height = 3.9, dpi = 150)
```

Attitudes towards politics and democracy that form in adolescence and early adulthood can last into later life. All four surveys asked about political interest and satisfaction with democracy, and three asked about trust in five institutions. Because the surveys cover different ages, we mostly compare age groups within a survey.

## Interest in politics

::: {.how-to-read}
Each line shows one survey. The dots give the share of respondents at each year of age who are fairly or very interested in politics. Ages with fewer than 20 respondents in a survey are left out.
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-interest
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-alt: "Share of respondents who are fairly or very interested in politics by year of age, from 12 to 26, for each survey. Within Gallup W2, the share rises from under 40% at age 16 to about 75% at age 26, and Gallup W1 shows a similar rise from 16 to 21. Within the two Survation surveys the share changes less with age. Survation W1 lies above Survation W2 at every age."
interest_age <- respondents |>
  summarise(share = mean(interested), n = n(), .by = c(dataset, age)) |>
  filter(n >= 20)

# label positions chosen by hand, so that no label crosses a line
interest_labels <- tribble(
  ~dataset, ~age, ~share,
  "Survation W1", 12, 0.665,
  "Survation W2", 12, 0.30,
  "Gallup W1", 21.3, 0.52,
  "Gallup W2", 26.3, 0.75
) |>
  mutate(dataset = factor(dataset, levels = names(dataset_colours)))

ggplot(interest_age, aes(x = age, y = share, colour = dataset)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  geom_text(
    data = interest_labels,
    aes(label = dataset),
    hjust = 0, size = 3.6, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dataset_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 12:26, limits = c(12, 28.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  labs(
    title = "Among Gallup respondents, interest in politics rises with age",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Fairly or very interested",
    caption = site_caption
  )
```

In Gallup W2, the only survey that covers ages 16 to 26, the share fairly or very interested in politics rises from `r interest_gw2[["16"]]` at age 16 to `r interest_gw2[["26"]]` at age 26. Gallup W1 shows a similar rise between 16 and 21. In Survation, by contrast, interest varies less between ages 12 and 17. The two Survation waves also differ, with `r interest[["Survation W1"]]` fairly or very interested in W1 but only `r interest[["Survation W2"]]` in W2. However, the `r n_sw1_panel` Survation W1 respondents who took part again a year later were less interested in W1 (`r interest_sw1_panel[["panel"]]`) than the others (`r interest_sw1_panel[["others"]]`), which suggests that the gap partly reflects who took part. Within each survey, young men report interest in politics slightly more often than young women, by `r interest_gap[1]` to `r interest_gap[2]` percentage points.

## Satisfaction with democracy

::: {.how-to-read}
Each bar shows the answers of young women or young men in one survey to the statement "I am satisfied with the way that democracy works in the United Kingdom", on a scale from 1 (fully disagree) to 7 (fully agree).
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-democracy
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-alt: "Stacked bars of the share of young women and young men who are dissatisfied (1 to 3), neutral (4) or satisfied (5 to 7) with the way democracy works in the UK, for each survey. In both Gallup surveys, more respondents are dissatisfied than satisfied, and young women are dissatisfied more often than young men. In Survation W1 more are satisfied than dissatisfied. In Survation W2 the three groups are of similar size."
swd_bars <- respondents |>
  filter(gender %in% c("Female", "Male")) |>
  mutate(
    answer = case_when(
      swdkep1 <= 3 ~ "Dissatisfied (1 to 3)",
      swdkep1 == 4 ~ "Neutral (4)",
      .default = "Satisfied (5 to 7)"
    ),
    answer = factor(answer, levels = c("Satisfied (5 to 7)", "Neutral (4)", "Dissatisfied (1 to 3)")),
    gender = fct_recode(gender, "Young women" = "Female", "Young men" = "Male")
  ) |>
  count(dataset, gender, answer) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n), .by = c(dataset, gender)) |>
  mutate(group = fct_rev(fct_inorder(str_c(dataset, ", ", str_to_lower(gender))))) |>
  arrange(dataset, gender)

ggplot(swd_bars, aes(x = share, y = group, fill = answer)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1), colour = answer),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
    size = 3.4,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Dissatisfied (1 to 3)" = brand[["coral-dark"]],
      "Neutral (4)" = brand[["rule"]],
      "Satisfied (5 to 7)" = brand[["blue-dark"]]
    ),
    breaks = c("Dissatisfied (1 to 3)", "Neutral (4)", "Satisfied (5 to 7)"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Dissatisfied (1 to 3)" = brand[["paper"]],
      "Neutral (4)" = brand[["ink"]],
      "Satisfied (5 to 7)" = brand[["paper"]]
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(), expand = expansion(0)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Young women are less often satisfied with democracy than young men",
    x = "Share of respondents",
    y = NULL,
    caption = site_caption
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    legend.location = "plot",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(5.5, 18, 5.5, 5.5)
  )
```

In both Gallup surveys, more young people are dissatisfied than satisfied with how democracy works in the UK (`r swd_stat("Gallup W1", "dissatisfied")` against `r swd_stat("Gallup W1", "satisfied")` in W1, and `r swd_stat("Gallup W2", "dissatisfied")` against `r swd_stat("Gallup W2", "satisfied")` in W2). Among the adolescents in Survation, more are satisfied than dissatisfied in W1, while in W2 the two groups are of similar size and `r swd_stat("Survation W2", "neutral")` choose the middle of the scale. In every survey, young women are satisfied less often than young men, for instance `r swd_g("Gallup W2", "Female")` against `r swd_g("Gallup W2", "Male")` in Gallup W2. Within Gallup W2, satisfaction is also more common among 22 to 26 year olds (`r swd_gw2_age[["22-26"]]`) than 18 to 21 year olds (`r swd_gw2_age[["18-21"]]`). Across the surveys, satisfaction goes together with interest, as `r swd_by_interest[["Very interested"]]` of those very interested in politics are satisfied, compared with `r swd_by_interest[["Not at all interested"]]` of those not at all interested.

## Trust in institutions

::: {.how-to-read}
Each row is one institution, and the dots give its average trust rating in each survey on a scale from 0 (no trust at all) to 10 (complete trust). Survation W2 did not ask these questions.
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-trust
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "Average trust in courts, police, the UK government, political parties and the media in Gallup W1, Survation W1 and Gallup W2. In every survey, the courts and the police receive the highest trust and political parties and the media the lowest. Survation W1 shows higher trust than the two Gallup surveys for every institution, and Gallup W2 slightly higher trust than Gallup W1."
trust_plot <- trust_means |>
  mutate(institution = fct_reorder(institution, mean))

ggplot(trust_plot, aes(x = mean, y = institution)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, colour = brand[["rule"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(group = institution), colour = brand[["rule"]], linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = dataset), shape = 21, size = 3.4, colour = brand[["ink"]], stroke = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = dataset_colours, breaks = c("Gallup W1", "Survation W1", "Gallup W2"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(3, 7), breaks = 3:7) +
  labs(
    title = "Courts and police are trusted more than parties and the media",
    x = "Average trust (0 none, 10 complete)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = site_caption
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    legend.location = "plot",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )
```

In every survey that asked about trust, the courts and the police are trusted most and political parties and the media least. In Gallup W1, for example, trust averages `r tm("Gallup W1", "Police")` for the police but `r tm("Gallup W1", "Political parties")` for political parties. Survation W1 shows higher trust in every institution, which fits its higher answers on all 0 to 10 scales. Gallup W1 was fielded under a Conservative government and Gallup W2 under a Labour one, yet among 18 to 21 year olds, the one age group both surveys cover well, trust in the UK government is almost the same (`r trust_gallup_age[["Gallup W1 18-21"]]` and `r trust_gallup_age[["Gallup W2 18-21"]]`). The higher Gallup W2 average thus comes mainly from its 22 to 26 year olds (`r trust_gallup_age[["Gallup W2 22-26"]]`). In both Gallup surveys, young men trust the government somewhat more than young women, for instance `r trust_gender_gov[["Gallup W2 Male"]]` against `r trust_gender_gov[["Gallup W2 Female"]]` in Gallup W2.

## Ways of governing

::: {.how-to-read}
Each row is one way of governing a country. The dots give the share of respondents in each survey who find it fairly or very good (5 to 7 on a scale from 1, very bad, to 7, very good).
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-governing
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-alt: "Share of respondents who rate six ways of governing as good, by survey. Elections where every vote is equal receive the most support, from about 70% to 90%. The three authoritarian ways, such as a strong leader who does not accept interference, are rated good by about a third to three fifths of respondents. Survation respondents rate a strong leader as good more often than Gallup respondents."
governing_items <- c(
  dem1_UK = "Elections where every vote is equal",
  dem2_UK = "Fundamental rights for everyone",
  dem3_UK = "Several groups can be elected",
  aut1_UK = "Strong leader without interference",
  aut2_UK = "Strong government using tough means",
  aut3_UK = "Less control over the government"
)

governing <- respondents |>
  select(dataset, all_of(names(governing_items))) |>
  pivot_longer(-dataset, names_to = "item", values_to = "rating") |>
  summarise(good = mean(rating >= 5), .by = c(dataset, item)) |>
  mutate(
    type = if_else(str_starts(item, "dem"), "Democratic", "Authoritarian"),
    type = factor(type, levels = c("Democratic", "Authoritarian")),
    item = factor(governing_items[item], levels = rev(governing_items))
  )

ggplot(governing, aes(x = good, y = item)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = item), colour = brand[["rule"]], linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = dataset), shape = 21, size = 3.4, colour = brand[["ink"]], stroke = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(type ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = dataset_colours, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(), limits = c(0.2, 1), breaks = seq(0.2, 1, 0.2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Most value equal votes, but many also find a strong leader appealing",
    x = "Rated fairly or very good",
    y = NULL,
    caption = site_caption
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    legend.location = "plot",
    strip.placement = "outside",
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 90, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )
```

Large majorities in all surveys find democratic ways of governing good, and elections where every vote counts equally receive the most support, from `r gd("Gallup W1", "dem1_UK")` in Gallup W1 to `r gd("Survation W1", "dem1_UK")` in Survation W1. At the same time, a strong leader who accepts no interference is rated good by `r gd("Gallup W1", "aut1_UK")` in Gallup W1, `r gd("Gallup W2", "aut1_UK")` in Gallup W2 and close to three fifths in both Survation surveys. These views can coexist, as `r gd("Survation W2", "both")` of Survation W2 respondents rate both equal elections and a strong leader as good. Some may read "strong leader" as effective leadership rather than a rejection of democratic checks, but these data cannot tell.

The samples are not weighted and the surveys differ in age range and recruitment, so differences between them should be read with care. [The data](/data.qmd) page describes how the surveys differ.
